rule: In a deload (and transition/reset) week run volume is 0.7x the current weekly mileage
summary: No trial tests a running 'down week' or its size; the 20-40% cut every 3-4 weeks is a coaching convention. A 30% cut is well below the 41-60% that taper meta-analyses find best for peaking, so it keeps aerobic stimulus while easing load, which suits a returning runner who must not lose the ramp. The strength-deload literature (Delphi consensus, surveys) supports reducing volume while keeping frequency, and Coleman 2024 suggests a complete break costs strength; it says nothing about the 0.7 number for running. Keep it as a labelled heuristic and check it against the athlete's data (next-week RPE, joint scores, readiness after deloads).

sources.note: Bosquet 2007: a 41-60% volume cut with intensity kept is the best taper; a 30% cut is a lighter, non-peaking reduction
Bell 2023 Delphi: deload = reduced training stress to mitigate fatigue; strength/physique only, no running dose
Rogerson 2024 survey: deloads cut volume while frequency stays unchanged (in lifters)
Coleman 2024: complete 1-wk cessation reduced strength gains vs continuous training, which favours a partial cut over stopping
